name: requirements-to-roadmap
goal: Convert ambitions into prioritized deliverable milestones with dependencies and verifiable outcomes.
when: Turning goals into programs, roadmaps, multi-team plans or delivery portfolios.
not_when: An isolated task can be executed immediately with no coordination.
steps: Identify outcome, constraints, stakeholders, scope exclusions and measurable success over the planning horizon.
Decompose into user-facing capabilities and infrastructure prerequisites; separate commitments from candidate ideas.
Establish dependencies, sequencing, critical path, integration points and operational risk.
Estimate uncertainty ranges and define milestones by accepted artifacts, not only effort burned.
Prioritize using impact, confidence, urgency and cost while recording explicit tradeoffs and owner decisions.
Publish roadmap with scope change, review cadence, quality gates and blocked-dependency protocol.
gate: Each committed milestone has owner, acceptance evidence and realistic prerequisite chain.
anti: No false precision in date estimates or roadmaps of features unrelated to customer outcomes.
blocked: If resource capacity is unknown, present scenario-based timing rather than fabricated deadlines.

name: openproject-delivery
goal: Operate OpenProject work packages with clear ownership, constraints and acceptance criteria.
when: Managing work packages, dependencies, milestones or releases in OpenProject.
not_when: User does not use OpenProject or need work management.
steps: Inventory project scope, work package types, roles, existing status workflow and permissions.
Translate goals into work packages with unique descriptions, acceptance conditions, owner and deliverable paths.
Link predecessor/dependent packages, milestones and risks while avoiding artificial excessive task granularity.
Configure dashboards and views for blockers, lead time, overdue dependencies, verification and launch readiness.
Update actual statuses only from verified progress and use comments to record decisions, changed scope and evidence.
Deliver package import/mapping and operating cadence with exception escalation rules.
gate: Critical path and accountability are visible; completed packages have attached acceptance evidence.
anti: Do not mark tasks done based on intention, manufacture project IDs or assume ungranted write permissions.
blocked: Without connected OpenProject access, provide importable files and instructions, not claims of creating tickets.

name: risk-register-governance
goal: Maintain actionable project and operational risk decisions with early-warning indicators.
when: Complex projects, vendor reliance, security review or high-impact launch readiness.
not_when: Tiny reversible task with no nontrivial uncertainty.
steps: Identify strategic, technical, schedule, supplier, privacy, financial and user-experience uncertainties.
Express each risk as cause, triggering event and measurable consequence rather than a vague label.
Assess probability and impact on a consistent scale; note confidence and correlated risks.
Define owner, mitigation, contingency, trigger indicators, budget and due date for top risks.
Review changes at meaningful milestones, closing retired risks and escalating threshold breaches.
Deliver register and decision summary with accepted residual exposures.
gate: Every high-rated risk has owner, meaningful action and escalation trigger.
anti: No identical “monitor risk” mitigation or false quantified probabilities without data.
blocked: When evidence is sparse, use ordinal ratings and confidence labels.

name: acceptance-quality-release
goal: Provide a cross-functional release gate based on evidence instead of subjective readiness.
when: Preparing launch sign-off, QA handoff, publication or production rollout.
not_when: Exploratory brainstorming with no output being released.
steps: Enumerate promised functionality, content/media deliverables, target platforms, compliance and support expectations.
Define critical acceptance cases for functionality, accessibility, security, performance, correctness and compatibility.
Collect traceable proof per case: test logs, inspected render, sign-off, source citations or reproducible measurements.
Separate pass, fail, blocked, not applicable and not tested statuses with severity and accountable owner.
Choose release, controlled rollback, staged rollout or hold based on nonnegotiable gates and residual exposure.
Publish release decision, rollback/readiness plan and postrelease observation window.
gate: No hard-blocking critical case is falsely marked passed; release sign-off is linked to observable proof.
anti: Never substitute a success-sounding narrative for actual tests or conceal unexecuted cases.
blocked: If proof is inaccessible, mark blocked/not tested and recommend scope reduction or hold appropriately.

name: customer-support-knowledge-base
goal: Build accurate support documentation and triage flows for user-facing systems.
when: Shipping help-center articles, onboarding support, runbooks or support agents.
not_when: Internal speculative product with no users yet.
steps: Collect frequent issues, product behavior, screenshots/versions, supported plans and escalation policy.
Structure articles around user task and symptom with prerequisites, recovery paths and observable success steps.
Separate troubleshooting facts from guesses and include safe stop/escalate criteria for account/security issues.
Write accessible concise steps with exact UI labels and version ownership; avoid exposing internal-only infrastructure or personal records.
Validate instructions on real product version and with representative novice users or support staff.
Deliver article collection, tagging/search terms, escalation routing and feedback loop for stale guidance.
gate: A user/support agent can reproduce the described resolution on supported versions without unsafe side effects.
anti: No invented menu names, fake error codes or articles that instruct disclosing passwords.
blocked: If UI is not available for verification, label steps as draft and require product review.

name: rea-capability-routing
goal: Select the narrowest evidence-producing REA workflow for a specified shipped artifact without unnecessary setup or unsafe execution
when: a user asks to inspect a shipped application, binary, recorded runtime, or captured web behavior and the available agent must decide how to connect REA
not_when: a user only needs a source repository explanation, ordinary code generation, or a general comparison of software products
steps: Define a proof obligation for the specific user question and decide whether source files already answer it; if so avoid REA.
Classify the artifact by bytes and packaging: ASAR/JS, APK, managed PE, native ELF/PE/Mach-O, archive/PyInstaller, firmware, HAR, or live browser; do not select from the filename alone.
Map the type to its target-free inspector or session-bound tool; use actual MCP tools/list and advertised schemas, never tools remembered from upstream main.
If the required tool is connected, make the minimum read-only call and capture its Evidence. Do not run doctor or setup as a ritual prerequisite.
When an observed blocker exists, distinguish client approval, MCP registration, engine prerequisite, timeout and platform support; collect read-only diagnostics before any proposed repair.
For a registration repair, show dry-run scoped paths and backups; obtain approval before changes. A completed setup still requires a client reconnection and confirmation that tools appear.
Record analyzed artifact hashes, selected providers, observation scope, unsupported features and exact next query; never replace the selected target with a nearby example.
artifacts: a target-to-tool routing decision and minimal readiness report
an evidence and permission boundary table
an explicit fallback if REA is not available
gate: The chosen operation matches the identified artifact and user authorization; tool availability is observed rather than assumed; no setup or target execution happens implicitly
anti: Treating skill installation as MCP installation, picking a native decompiler for a JS tree, or running global setup for a single missing tool
blocked: If REA is missing, use a permitted local read-only inspection or describe precisely which capability is unavailable. Do not claim an REA Evidence record was produced.
inputs: the explicitly supplied artifact path or owned target endpoint and the question it must answer
host platform, actual connected tool list, installed REA version if known, and current permissions
whether passive inspection, application execution, network access, or filesystem writes are allowed
special_rules: An ASAR or extracted Electron/JavaScript tree routes to `analyze_javascript_application`, not `open_binary`.
Android code routes to `inspect_android_package`; archive membership of an APK is a separate inventory question.
Managed PE routes to `inspect_managed_artifact`; NativeAOT routes to native analysis if supported.
A saved HAR routes to `inspect_web_network_capture`; a declared browser action routes to `capture_browser_scenario`.
REA registration, native providers, and captured data permissions are separate checks.

name: handoff
goal: Write a durable, self-contained handoff file that lets a fresh agent resume this session's work without chat history.
when: The user asks to hand off or transfer the session to another agent, checkpoint the session, or save its context or continuation notes for later.
not_when: The user only wants a plan, notes or other content saved to a project file, or a deliverable's next-owner summary within another workflow.
steps: Read `references/handoff-contract.md`, then choose the destination in its order: an existing repository `handoffs/` (preferred) or `.codex/handoffs/`, otherwise a new repository `handoffs/`, otherwise `/tmp/agent-handoffs/`, named `<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md`; for repo-local files record both the repo-relative path and the original absolute path.

Inspect actual state rather than memory: timestamp, working directory, repository root, branch, HEAD, `git status --short`, `git diff --name-only`, `git diff --cached --name-only`, relevant diffs or excerpts, and active background commands, subagents, worktrees, temporary files or generated artifacts; outside Git, record that fact and gather the equivalent filesystem context.

Reconstruct the latest user request and still-binding earlier constraints, then list commands run with observed outcomes, including skipped or failed checks; separate completed facts, work in progress, planned next steps, assumptions and open questions.

Write the file before responding, with the contract's sections in order: Resume Prompt, Current Goal, Current State, User Requests And Constraints, Work Completed, Work In Progress, Changed Files, Verification, Known Issues Or Blockers, Next Actions and Context Notes.

Make the Resume Prompt self-contained: for repo-local files it tells the next agent, from the repository root, to read the repo-relative handoff path first, verify the current repository state, then continue from Next Actions without relying on prior chat history; use absolute paths only for provenance, external files or non-repository handoffs.

Re-read the written file against the acceptance gate: every section present and ordered, no secrets or hidden instructions, no verification claim without an observed command, and no file other than the handoff touched unless the user asked.
Respond with the absolute handoff path, the exact resume prompt, and any inspection or verification step that could not be completed.

self-contained resume prompt that uses a repo-relative path for repo-local handoffs

name: git-checkpoint
goal: Turn already-completed work into reviewable local Git commits without absorbing unrelated changes, bypassing hooks or pushing.
when: The user explicitly asks to commit, create a local Git checkpoint, or prepare focused local commits from an existing working tree.
not_when: The user has not asked for a commit, wants a session continuation file rather than a Git commit, or asks to push, publish, merge, amend, rebase or release.
steps: Read `references/checkpoint-contract.md`, confirm the request explicitly authorizes local commits, and collect read-only Git evidence (prefer `gitevidence`): branch, upstream, HEAD, dirty and staged state and diff summary; stop and report on unmerged paths, unclear file ownership, a needed history rewrite, or a review-only request.

Check verification currency: evidence counts only if it ran after the relevant edits, covers the changed files' risk and was not invalidated by a later formatter, generator or manual edit; otherwise run `change-verify` when the request allows, or report the commit as unverified and never as verified.

Plan dependency-complete logical commits (prefer `commit_plan operation=plan`): source with its tests, schema or config with its consumers, docs with their behavior and maintenance separately; never knowingly leave an intermediate commit broken or mix in unrelated cleanup, and refine every starter message to the actual change.

Before each commit confirm the exact file list and inspect staged and unstaged hunks for secrets, generated noise, debug artifacts and unrelated files, then apply with `commit_plan operation=apply` or explicit-path staging; never use `git add .`, `git add -A` or another blanket stage.

Let hooks run: on a hook failure preserve its output and stop without `--no-verify`, inspect any files a hook modified, and never repeat a mutating Git command whose outcome is unknown before confirming HEAD and status read-only.
After every commit capture its short SHA and subject and confirm unrelated changes remain untouched; after the last, run `gitevidence` and `gitverify` before any readiness claim.

Report with the contract's output table: authorization, verification status, each commit's SHA, message, files and verification, remaining and preserved changes, hook results, the parent plan's remaining outcomes and return point, and that nothing was pushed or published.
artifacts: Local commits that each carry one coherent intent with a reviewed message
checkpoint report giving SHA, message, files and verification status per commit
statement of remaining changes, preserved unrelated changes, hook results and push status (not performed)
gate: Every commit was explicitly authorized, staged only reviewed explicit paths, passed its hooks without bypass, left unrelated changes untouched, and is reported with its SHA and an honest current, partial or missing verification status; nothing was pushed.
anti: Never commit without being asked, blanket-stage a dirty tree, split source from the tests that make it valid, bypass or retry around a failed hook, amend, rebase, reset, clean, force or push, or call work ready because a commit succeeded.
blocked: If `commit_plan` or `gitevidence` is unavailable, stage explicit paths, review `git diff --cached --stat` and the staged diff, and confirm state with read-only Git commands; if authorization, file ownership or verification is unclear, stop and report instead of committing.
inputs: the user's explicit commit or checkpoint request and its scope
current branch, HEAD, staged and unstaged diff, and pre-existing unrelated changes
verification evidence for the final file state

name: change-verify
goal: Prove with repository-defined, risk-proportionate checks what an existing code or documentation change does and does not establish, without repairing it.
when: A code or documentation change already exists and must be verified before claiming completion, committing, publishing or handing work off.
not_when: The task is to implement or repair code, design a new test strategy, troubleshoot build infrastructure, review a diff for findings, or sign off a product release.
steps: Read `references/verification-contract.md`, then inspect the working-tree and staged diff (prefer `gitevidence`): classify changed paths as source, tests, docs, config, generated or dependency, note API, schema, build, security, concurrency or persistence boundaries, and separate task-owned from pre-existing or unrelated changes.

Fix finite required gates from the contract's risk ladder before running anything, deriving each command from repository instructions, manifests, CI or verifier profiles (`codegraph_affected`, `test_gap_planner`, `test_runner infer`, `lsp diagnostics`); never invent a likely command, and treat stale or degraded graph or LSP output as a reason to broaden.

Budget fixtures, logs and expensive runs with explicit ownership and retention, then run the cheapest relevant targeted check first through `test_runner run`, `test_project` or `build_project`; follow `long-run` for long checks instead of sleep and tail polling.

On failure capture the first actionable error, classify it as in scope, pre-existing, environmental or unknown, do not rerun it unchanged, and report the failed gate, affected outcomes and checks not reached; do not repair it here, while an enclosing authorized implementation plan keeps its own repair authority.

When targeted checks pass, run the broader gates the risk ladder and repository policy require (prefer an applicable `verification_center` profile), without launching a costly full suite for a low-risk change unless instructions or uncertainty demand it.

Run `gitverify` before any readiness claim and re-read the changed-file list so formatter or generator output is caught; confirm only intended files changed, no conflict markers or accidental artifacts exist, and results correspond to the final file state.

Report PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL with the contract's gate table, unrelated changes, not-run checks, residual risk and the parent return point; only PASS supports a verified, ready-to-commit or ready-to-publish claim.
artifacts: Verification result (PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL) with change scope and risk class
gate table giving each check's command or scope, result and evidence
list of unrelated changes, not-run checks, residual risk and the parent return point
gate: Every required gate was derived from repository sources and either ran against the final file state or is reported as failed or not run, `gitverify` or its stated fallback ran last, and PASS is claimed only when every required gate passed.
anti: Never repair code while verifying, run the full suite before a cheap targeted check, choose convenient rather than affected tests, rerun an unexplained failure hoping it passes, weaken assertions, silently update snapshots, bypass hooks, or omit failed and skipped commands.
blocked: If test inference, affected-test graphs or managed verifiers are unavailable, use commands cited by repository docs, CI or manifests and choose conservatively; if a verifier times out, inspect the process before classifying the result, and never turn unavailable evidence into a pass.
inputs: the existing change: working-tree and staged diff
repository instructions, manifests, CI workflows and verifier profiles
the required outcomes the verification must support

name: long-run
goal: Own one long-running process from launch or attachment to a clear milestone or terminal verdict through managed jobs instead of ad hoc sleep and tail polling.
when: A build, full test suite, server, training run, download, generation or pretokenization job may outlive a normal tool call or needs readiness or progress milestones.
not_when: The command finishes within a normal tool call, or the task is application logging or production observability design, experiment-hypothesis design, or fixing a build system.
steps: Read `references/long-run-contract.md` and write the run contract before launch: exact command and working directory, duration class, owned outputs and log path, readiness or progress milestone, terminal success and failure conditions, bounded observation window and cleanup; for experiments check `experiment_ledger` first and never rerun a settled arm.

Choose the manager from the contract's table: `bg_run` for builds, full suites, generators and servers; `run_deck launch` for training, downloads, pretokenization and recurring metrics; `run_deck attach` for an externally started run; `experiment_ledger` plus `run_deck` for arms with pass bars.

Launch or attach exactly once and retain the job or run ID and log path; never start a second copy because status is quiet, and before any relaunch confirm the original process is dead or intentionally stopped.

Make one bounded startup check, using `run_deck watch` with a specific milestone pattern for a near-term milestone, and classify the state as started, ready or progressing, finished, failed or unknown; a watch timeout means not observed, not failed.

On later turns query status once and report only new evidence such as exit state, progress, loss or throughput indicators, readiness, resource pressure or the first actionable error; when the user asked for periodic notification, start one `run_monitor` over the retained ID and end the turn instead of polling. Its terminal checks are script-backed and never start a model turn.

Conclude from process state, exit status and required outputs rather than one log line: record concise evidence, `run_deck finish` registered runs with their final status and metrics, judge partial artifacts, stop only the owned job when required, and report where logs are retained.
artifacts: Run contract stating command, milestone, deadline and success and failure conditions
long-run report giving manager and ID, state, latest evidence, verdict, logs and next observation or cleanup
gate: Exactly one owned process was launched or attached under a retained ID, its state is classified from process status plus required outputs or milestones rather than a single log line, and a bounded timeout is reported as unobserved rather than as failure or success.
anti: Never block on a full build or suite in an ordinary call, poll with shell sleep, tail or nvidia-smi loops, launch duplicates after a quiet interval, declare success from log text, kill by executable name or broad pattern, or store raw logs or secrets in durable notes.
blocked: If no managed background tool exists, use the contract's bounded fallback: one background process with a recorded PID, a task-owned log and exit-status file, increasing poll intervals and a fixed deadline, stopping only that PID, and report that lifecycle guarantees are degraded.
inputs: the exact command, working directory and expected duration
required readiness, progress or completion milestones
the user's observation deadline and cleanup expectations

name: durable-bug-hunt
goal: Diagnose and repair an observed defect with a durable cross-session record of hypotheses, attempts and verdicts so failed fixes are never repeated.
when: A bug, crash, regression or flaky failure needs evidence-driven diagnosis and repair in a harness with `debug_ledger` attempt tracking, especially when it is intermittent, resurfaced or earlier fixes failed.
not_when: No defect has been observed, or the task is feature work, a broad audit, routine verification, or performance tuning without a correctness symptom.
steps: Read `references/bug-hunt-contract.md`, open or inspect the matching `debug_ledger` thread before changing anything, and check `fix_recall` for related failures; never retry a change already recorded as no-change, worse or an equivalent unresolved observation.

Record the bug contract (observed and expected behavior, exact failure signature, frequency and environment, smallest known reproduction, prior attempts and available logs or traces, attaching fresh captures via `evidence_inbox`), and reproduce or narrow before repair, marking non-reproduction honestly.

Map the failure path from the failing boundary, callers, invariants, tests and recent changes, classify the failure family (logic, lifecycle, ownership, concurrency, configuration, dependency or measurement), and for native crashes use the repository build and test tools that capture backtraces.

Use normal mode for a new reproducible defect and deep mode when it is intermittent, resurfaced, low-confidence or previously failed; record each hypothesis's causal claim, supporting and conflicting evidence, falsification test, confidence and result, with at least three materially different hypotheses in deep mode.

Fix only when one mechanism explains the symptom better than the alternatives and the violated invariant is located: take a `safe_try` checkpoint for risky changes, change one causal variable, run the narrow reproduction, record the observation and verdict in the ledger, and revert on worse.

Run targeted then justified broader regression checks, inspect the diff for defensive masking or unrelated cleanup, and resolve the ledger only when the original reproduction passes, regression protection exists and broader checks did not regress.

Report with the contract's output: bug, mode, ledger thread, reproduction status, root cause or unresolved gap, attempt and verdict, evidence, PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL verification and residual uncertainty.
artifacts: `debug_ledger` thread with every hypothesis, attempt, observation and verdict
root-cause causal chain or an explicitly unresolved evidence gap
minimal fix with targeted regression evidence and stated residual uncertainty
gate: The ledger was checked before any change, no recorded failed attempt was repeated, the fix removes an identified mechanism confirmed by the original reproduction and a regression check, and the thread is resolved only on that current evidence.
anti: Never patch speculatively, stack another guess on a worse result, mask defects with retries, sleeps, broad guards, swallowed errors or fallbacks, treat a tool or provider failure as evidence about the product defect, claim root cause from one lucky pass, or refactor broadly during the hunt.
blocked: If the ledger tools are unavailable, keep an explicit attempt table with hypothesis, change, observation, verdict and evidence in the session or an approved handoff artifact; if indexed context or managed verifiers are unavailable, use focused search and canonical test commands, and never treat missing tooling as confirmation.
inputs: the observed failure signature, expected behavior and environment
reproduction steps, logs, traces or verifier output

name: experiment-gate-lifecycle
goal: Run a pre-registered experiment through validity gates, managed runs, recorded verdicts and an explicit ship, no-go or shelved decision without losing bars, null results or cost history.
when: A research or engineering experiment, A/B arm, field cohort, prototype, benchmark or falsification loop must be pre-registered and gated with `experiment_ledger`, or an open experiment record needs its next gate or closure.
not_when: The task only designs an experiment's statistics or sampling, manages a process without pass bars, selects among generative models, or is still inventing the hypothesis or framework.
steps: Read `references/experiment-gate-contract.md`, inspect open `experiment_ledger` records before launching anything, and classify the request as new, continuation, reframe or settled; keep a continuation's registered bars and arms exactly and never rerun a settled question unchanged.

Pre-register with `experiment_ledger open`: one falsifiable hypothesis, exact arms, cheap deterministic gates before expensive ones, numerical pass bars and kill criteria, the cost and time envelope and the final ship gate, using `experiment-design-analysis` for estimands, power and randomization; if no meaningful bar can be written, the experiment is not ready.

Prove validity before measuring the hypothesis (build parity, units and fixtures, seed and input parity, baseline reproducibility, privacy and mutation boundaries); a failed validity gate is recorded, fixed once and rerun alone, never counted as a hypothesis result.

Launch each arm once through a managed tool (`run_deck` for training, downloads, generation and metrics; `bg_run` for builds, suites and servers; `run_monitor` only on request), retaining run IDs and log paths and checking status before any relaunch.

Record every gate with `experiment_ledger gate`: label, pass, fail, null-result or partial verdict, measured numbers against the registered bar, run ID and commit, GPU-hours or other cost and a concise interpretation; never weaken a bar after seeing results.

Classify poor results as implementation failure, measurement failure, hypothesis failure or null result; allow one repair rerun for implementation or measurement failures, and never tune a failed hypothesis without a materially changed arm or a reframe.

Close with `experiment_ledger close`: ship only when every ship gate passes, no-go when decisive evidence rejects the direction, shelved when evidence is incomplete and no bounded next experiment is justified; cite final evidence and state what must not be retried unchanged.
artifacts: Pre-registered `experiment_ledger` record with hypothesis, arms, bars, kill criteria and cost bound
gate verdicts with measured values, run IDs and cost
explicit ship, no-go or shelved decision with the next bounded action
gate: Hypothesis, arms, bars and cost bound were registered before the first run and never weakened, every material run and gate verdict including failures and null results is linked to the record, and the decision follows the registered gates rather than process exit status.
anti: Never launch before pre-registration, treat broken plumbing as evidence against the hypothesis, report only successful arms, repeat a null or failed arm unchanged, tune before the central mechanism shows signal, or close from process exit status instead of gate metrics.
blocked: If `experiment_ledger` or managed run tools are unavailable, write the pre-registration, gate table and decision to a repository-approved file before any run, mark unobserved gates NOT TESTED, and do not substitute shell polling loops for managed runs.
inputs: the hypothesis or open experiment ID with prior decisions
available arms, baselines, fixtures and the compute or cost budget

name: build
goal: Diagnose and fix repository build, toolchain, dependency, sanitizer, static-analysis and CI failures from the repository's own build contract without hiding failures.
when: A configure, compile, link, dependency-resolution, sanitizer, static-analysis or CI build step fails, or compiler, toolchain or build-system settings must change, in CMake, npm, Cargo, Python or mixed-language repositories.
not_when: The task is designing release, packaging or deployment pipelines, merely running a long build, verifying a finished change, or debugging runtime behavior of a program that already builds.
steps: Read `references/build-contract.md`, then identify the build contract from manifests, lockfiles, build files, CI workflows, tool versions and repository instructions: canonical command, target and configuration, toolchain versions, dependency policy, caches and generated artifacts, and local-versus-CI differences.

Classify the failure as configure or manifest, dependency resolution or lock drift, compile or typecheck, link, package or bundle, test invocation or discovery, sanitizer or static analysis, or CI environment such as permissions, disk, memory, timeout or provider; a provider or resource failure is not a source failure.

Reproduce the exact failing target and configuration with `build_project`, `test_runner` or checked-in scripts rather than guessed command lines, capture the first causal error rather than downstream cascades, and run long builds as `long-run` managed jobs.

Apply the smallest durable change to checked-in configuration or source (target-scoped flags, existing pinned dependencies, explicit version constraints) using the contract's CMake, npm, Cargo and Python checks; never suppress warnings, disable tests or sanitizers, pin arbitrary old versions or add fallback toolchains or parallel build paths.

Rerun the original failing target and configuration, then the nearest broader build or CI check, confirming that cache or generated state is not the only reason it passes and that local and CI configurations remain aligned.
Report the build target, canonical command, failure class, root cause, changed files with rationale, PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL verification, CI parity and residual environment assumptions.
artifacts: Failure classification with a first-cause root-cause statement
minimal checked-in build, configuration or source change with rationale
build report with canonical command, verification result, CI parity and environment assumptions
gate: The original failing target and configuration now pass through the repository-defined command, the nearest broader build or CI check passes, and no warning, test, sanitizer or lockfile was disabled, suppressed or deleted to get there.
anti: Never treat the last error as the first cause, add global flags for one target, hand-write a new build path before checking existing scripts, claim success from a different configuration, or delete lockfiles or caches as the final fix.
blocked: If the failing environment such as a CI runner, toolchain version or hardware cannot be reproduced locally, state the exact difference, fix only what local evidence supports, mark CI parity as a gap, and never claim an unobserved CI job passes.

build files, manifests, lockfiles and CI workflow definitions
toolchain versions and local versus CI environment differences

name: typesafe-ai
goal: Build AI-powered features with TypeSafe System One models such as Jev, turning natural language and application state into typed judgments and probabilities that code composes.
when: The user names TypeSafe or Jev, or a project using or evaluating TypeSafe needs programmable common sense for routing, ranking, extraction, verification or interactive decisions, or an LLM prompt-and-parse step to become a typed judgment.
not_when: The task needs free-form text generation, retrieval-augmented chat over private documents, or a vendor-neutral comparison of generative models, or TypeSafe is neither named nor in use.
steps: Read `references/typesafe-guide.md`, then treat the live docs as the source of truth: start at `https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt`, fetch pages as Markdown by appending `.md`, and before writing an integration read the current API or chosen SDK page, the relevant question guidance and the closest cookbook.

Start from what the application must show, select, change or hand off and work backward to the judgments it needs; keep known rules, calculations, exact lookups and execution in code, and preserve the user's stack and scope.

Choose a shape (route and fill arguments, select instead of generate, find and judge evidence, turn judgments into reusable scores, verify and escalate, or respond to changing state), offering a few directions for open-ended requests and building directly for concrete ones.

Design each question as one narrow judgment with the right primitive (Choice for one of a defined set, Noul for whether a condition holds, Score for degree along a dimension), enough named state, instructions plus criteria, a no-match outcome where nothing may fit, and full candidate coverage for selection.

Ask independent questions over the same state together and use a second request only when an earlier answer is needed; set probability and confidence thresholds from the user's data and consequences rather than cookbook defaults, keep policy explicit, and keep API credentials server-side.

Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior; for failures inspect state, questions, candidates, answers and composition, and separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors and service failures.

anti: Never invent version-dependent API details, generate text where selecting a judged candidate works, cram independent judgments into one question, treat confidence as permission to act or typed output as truth, or apply cookbook thresholds as universal rules.
